composition: Nominal composition is Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.8 C (wt%), a low-density austenitic Fe-Mn-Al-C steel; the actual composition measured after solutionization is Fe-30.6Mn-9.1Al-0.79 C. Manganese (the major alloying addition) stabilizes the austenite phase, aluminium lowers the density (measured 6.8 g/cm³ by Archimedes' principle), and carbon (0.79 wt%) provides interstitial solid-solution strengthening together with the κ-carbide-forming tendency of the Fe-Mn-Al-C system. Carbon was quantified by combustion infrared detection (LECO CS744); the other elements by wet chemical analysis.
conclusions: MAF-1 demonstrates that a single warm multiaxial forging pass at 250 °C is already a highly effective strengthening step: the yield strength of the solution-treated Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.8 C low-density steel is raised roughly threefold (380 → 1040 MPa) and the UTS from 762 to 1368 MPa, at the cost of ductility falling from 75% to 30%. Microstructurally the pass acts mainly through a large dislocation-density increase (~7× MAF-0) with only a modest grain-size refinement (50 → 35 μm), and the strengthening decomposition (531 MPa dislocation vs 129 MPa grain refinement) confirms that at low strain (early passes, 1–3) dislocation strengthening dominates over grain-boundary strengthening. The pass is part of a systematic MAF series (MAF-0/MAF-1/MAF-3/MAF-5 up to equivalent strain 2.3) in which MAF-3 reaches 1289 MPa and MAF-5 reaches 1528 MPa, while elongation falls to 8% and grain-boundary strengthening becomes relatively more important at later stages. The presented data underline the strength-ductility trade-off of warm MAF in low-density steel and provide the low-strain anchor point for validating a modified Johnson–Cook constitutive model that embeds strain-dependent dislocation density and grain size, which is intended to be transferable to other cold-deformation processes.
mechanisms: Warm MAF at 250 °C introduces 33% normal strain (equivalent strain ≈0.47) in one pass; because the temperature is low, thermally driven dislocation climb and cross-slip are partially suppressed, reducing dislocation mobility and dislocation annihilation at grain boundaries, so the equivalent strain and dislocation density build up rapidly (ρ rises to 5.57×10¹⁵ m⁻², about seven times the solution-treated value).

The imposed plastic strain promotes grain subdivision: dislocation accumulation organizes into a dense low-angle subgrain network inside the original grains, raising the low-angle boundary fraction from 0.367 (MAF-0) to 0.708 and lowering the high-angle fraction from 0.622 to 0.292, while the average grain size falls only modestly from 50 to 35 μm.

Strengthening at the first pass is dominated by dislocation (Taylor-type) strengthening rather than grain-boundary (Hall-Petch) strengthening: of the yield-strength increase over MAF-0, 531 MPa comes from the dislocation-density difference and only 129 MPa from grain refinement, producing the near threefold rise to 1040 MPa.

The rapid increase in dislocation density and microstrain consumes the material's work-hardening capacity, so the difference between yield strength and UTS shrinks (work-hardening amount drops from 392 to 328 MPa) and the ductility collapses from 75% to 30% total elongation.

Deformation proceeds by dislocation glide and accumulation without deformation twinning; local misorientation therefore rises (KAM average 0.72° versus 0.34° for MAF-0), consistent with stored-strain accumulation governed by dislocation processes rather than twinning.

The initial strong annealing texture (normal direction parallel to [101], with a secondary [111] component) is progressively broken up by the multi-directional forging flow, so after one pass many crystallographic directions lie parallel to the pressing direction and the XRD-preferred orientation shifts from (111) to (220); continued randomisation is expected to make the material more isotropic and stronger.

Because the κ-carbide reflections and the overall single-phase austenitic constitution are unchanged by MAF, precipitation and solid-solution strengthening contributions remain constant, so the entire yield-strength gain at this pass is attributable to dislocation density and grain size.
microstructure: MAF-1 retains a single-phase (majority austenite, γ, FCC) microstructure that is deformed and progressively subdivided relative to the solution-treated state. Average grain size from EBSD is 35 μm (down from 50 μm in MAF-0); XRD gives an average crystallite size of 13.4 nm. Grains are deformed and elongated and contain a dense low-angle subgrain network. The solution-treated material was strongly textured with normal direction parallel to [101], whereas after one pass the texture is broken up/randomized so that many different crystallographic directions lie parallel to the pressing direction; XRD intensity switches from a dominant (111) reflection in MAF-0 to a (220) preferred orientation in MAF-1. Grain boundaries are dominated by low-angle boundaries: the 1°–15° low-angle fraction rises drastically to 0.708 (from 0.367 in MAF-0) and the 15°–180° high-angle fraction falls to 0.292 (from 0.622). A negligible annealing-twin boundary fraction of 0.007 is present. Dislocation density reaches 5.57×10¹⁵ m⁻² with an average microstrain (e²)^1/2 of 5.18×10⁻³ (versus 0.79×10¹⁵ m⁻² and 3.66×10⁻³ for MAF-0), and the average KAM rises to 0.72° (from 0.34°). The grain-size distribution, initially wide, begins to narrow. κ-carbide reflections (κ(220), κ(222)) are present and unchanged before and after MAF, and a weak δ(211) feature appears near 95–105° 2θ; no new phase forms.
processing: A 2.5 kg ingot of Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.8 C was prepared by vacuum induction melting (Mn added after argon injection into the melt chamber at 600 mbar). The cast ingot was homogenized at 1200 °C for 2 h, then hot forged between 1200 and 900 °C with intermediate reheating to more than 60% deformation and water quenched. The forged material was then solutionized at 1050 °C for 1 h and water quenched to retain the maximum austenite fraction; this solution-treated state is the parent process (yielding MAF-0). For MAF, the ingot was cut into 30×20×20 mm rectangular billets, placed in a die with a 32×20 mm groove, and deformed along three mutually perpendicular directions on a 100-ton hydraulic press. Sample and die were heated to 250 °C and soaked for 2 h; the ram moved at a constant speed of 1 mm/s; specimens were fully lubricated with MoS₂ before pressing. Compression of the 30 mm height to 20 mm gives 33% normal strain per compression (equivalent strain ≈0.47 for one pass); the one-pass condition is denoted MAF-1. 250 °C was chosen because the alloy has its highest malleability between 150 and 450 °C, below the recrystallization temperature, and because deformation above ~450 °C would precipitate carbides, raising hardness and lowering ductility.
properties: Mechanical testing used miniature round tensile specimens (gauge length 16 mm, overall length 26.5 mm, gauge Ø4 mm, shoulder Ø7.2 mm, fillet radius R1, two specimens per condition) cut from the analysed region of the forged billet and tested at room temperature (reference 27 °C) in air at a strain rate of 1×10⁻³ s⁻¹ on an INSTRON hydraulic universal testing machine. MAF-1 shows a yield strength of 1040 MPa, an ultimate tensile strength of 1368 MPa and a total elongation of 30%; the Young's modulus is 160,000 MPa and density 6.8 g/cm³. The amount of work hardening is 328 MPa. Relative to the solution-treated MAF-0, the yield strength increases roughly threefold (from 380 MPa), UTS rises from 762 MPa, total elongation drops sharply from 75%, and the work-hardening amount falls from 392 MPa. The strengthening increment for MAF-1 decomposes into 531 MPa from the dislocation-density difference and 129 MPa from grain refinement. Characterization techniques applied to this sample include X-ray diffraction (Co-Kα radiation, 2° per minute, 0.02° step, 2θ = 40–120°, instrumental broadening subtracted using standard silicon), electron backscattered diffraction (image-quality, IPF and KAM maps, 60 μm scale bars), tensile testing, and 3D FEM simulation with a modified Johnson-Cook model. The engineering stress–strain curve of MAF-1 (red curve in Fig. 10) starts between 1000 and 1200 MPa, rises to a maximum between 1200 and 1400 MPa at strain ≈0.25, and fractures near strain 0.3.
summary: MAF-1 is a Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.8 C low-density steel (density 6.8 g/cm³) that was subjected to one pass of warm multiaxial forging (MAF) at 250 °C after a homogenization + hot forging + 1050 °C solution-treatment/water-quench pedigree. One MAF pass imposes 33% normal strain (equivalent strain ≈0.47) by sequential compression along three mutually perpendicular directions. The study asks how this first, low-strain warm deformation stage changes microstructure (dislocation density, grain size/substructure, texture) and tensile strength, and it serves as the first forged condition against which a modified Johnson–Cook / FEM framework for warm MAF is validated.
unmapped: 3D FEM (ABAQUS/Explicit) simulation of the MAF process for MAF-1 gives a maximum central-region equivalent strain of about 0.6, exceeding the applied external strain of 0.46, i.e. the centre of the billet is more severely deformed than the nominal value; the model reproduces the characteristic 'X'-shaped deformation pattern but does not exactly match the experimental billet distortion, a discrepancy attributed to the absence of crystallographic texture effects in the simulation.

The modified Johnson-Cook material model used for this steel embeds Eq. (6) with six VUMAT state-dependent variables (SDV1-6: equivalent plastic strain, equivalent plastic strain rate, dislocation density ρ_f, flow stress σ_flow, yield strength σ_y, grain size d_f) and uses input parameters σ_0 = 380 MPa, B = 1860 MPa, n = 1.02, m = 0.87, C = 0.0067, k = 2374 MPa·μm^0.5, k1 = 7.9×10¹⁵ m⁻², k2 = 1.8, k3 = 0.63, Poisson's ratio 0.3, melting temperature 1450 °C and reference temperature 27 °C.

The Fe-30Mn-9Al-0.8 C alloy in the solution-treated state has a very high room-temperature ductility (>70%, and greater than 95% at 300 °C) and good formability, which motivated its selection as a candidate low-density automotive steel capable of reducing vehicle weight, fuel consumption and CO2 emissions.
